newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: S.Leone coup head names council despite deal report.
newsitem.headline: S.Leone coup head names council despite deal report.

text.p: Negotiators maintain they have struck a deal with coupmakers to restore Sierra Leone's ousted civilian president but the new military strongman went ahead with naming his ruling council.
Diplomats hosting talks with the army played down Sunday's radio announcement, saying they still expected a deal to be signed.
Major Johnny Paul Koromah announced a 20-member council, with rebel leader Foday Sankoh as vice chairman and including three more members of Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front (RUF).

Koromah was the highest ranked of the original coup leaders but his policy-making body includes three brigadiers and four colonels, plus a few civilians, including the secretary-general of the government and the attorney-general.
The statement said the cabinet would be announced later.
But a senior Western diplomat said the announcement of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council was meant to reassure the army's lower ranks and the RUF which opposed negotiations.

"As they say, it's rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic," said the diplomat. "We expect an agreement to be reached and if the RUF opposes it, the regional force will go for them." Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea have sent troops ready for a military strike if the talks fail.
A unit of Nigerian troops in Sierra Leone came under fire from rebels on Sunday on the highway into the capital from Hastings airport to the east of town. No one was hurt.
British High Commissioner Peter Penfold and Nigerian High Commissioner Chidi Abubakar had hosted secret preliminary talks culminating in a comprehensive meeting on Sunday.
"The latest is that a deal has been cut. Everything should be in place in a day or two," a senior diplomat told Reuters.
The diplomat said Sankoh's rebels, who have been fighting a bush war since 1991 and have allied with the coupmakers, opposed a settlement and had not been part of the negotiations.
Under the agreement, a Nigerian-led force assembling in Freetown since last Sunday's coup would deploy to secure key points and keep order in the capital.

Diplomats said the RUF's resistance to a deal had already led to serious rifts between its commanders and the coup leaders. Sierra Leonean sources said two people had been killed in gunfights between RUF rebels and soldiers inside Koromah's military headquarters on a Freetown beachfront.
On Sunday U.S. helicopters evacuated the last Americans and Europeans who had taken refuge in two beachside hotels from the violence which followed the coup.
Britain chartered a DC10 to fly some 230 British evacuees from the Guinean capital Conakry on Sunday to London's Stansted airport.

Among the first to emerge when the plane landed early on Monday were three-year-old twins Daphne and Desphelia Lewis, who had returned to Britain alone, the British Press Association news agency reported.
The agency quoted British missionary Christine Jones, 49, as saying: "It was getting more and more tense by the time we got out on a French naval ship on Saturday.
"Since the situation became international, people who are not Sierra Leone nationals have become targets and homes are being looted.
"I saw a lot of shooting. I saw bodies and I saw shops just being cleared out. For quite a while I thought I would not get out alive."
